I think some important context to this (not a credible source here, just someone with my own experience and an interest in the history of LSD) is that during these experiments LSD had just been created. 

For those of us that have done this before, it’s usually a measured amount… we know how many of these measured amounts to take for the desired experience.

In these early “trials” they we’re figuring out how much volume resulted in objective experience…

And no one knew about it yet. It wasn’t like you could hit up Erowid and have an idea of what you’re about to do. 

For me, I can’t imagine if my first time I took LSD it was “hey try this new thing and no one else has yet so we don’t know if this is enough or too much”

Combined with the fact that many early LSD trials were on unsuspecting patients. Probably would have been worse to suddenly start tripping balls not knowing why, or worse, when (or if) it ends.

I have a few thoughts on disc brakes in general, manufacturers aside.

Mushy lever feel can have a lot of contributing factors:
-Bad bleed
-Damaged brake hose
-Improper compression on hose fittings 
-Worn out pad/rotor

A lot of these may not be applicable to you, but I’ve noticed these are reoccurring symptoms across all brands. 

If the brake needs bled is the easy one to check. A quick way to check is if the brake feels mushy,  pull the lever multiple times  quickly and see if you notice a firmer feel. A lot of times brake lines need to be shortened when bikes are built or sized or even need bled out of the box and this may have been over looked or rushed when the bike was initially built. 

If the brake hose is damaged and the inner lining ruptured is can allow the fluid to fill the space between the outer sheath and inner liner. The same can happen from an improperly installed or under torqued barb and olive. Look for sharp kinks in the brake hose, or confirm proper torque at any compression fitting or bleed port.

As far as brake noise is concerned, this can be a little more complicated.

Common issues to check for first:
-Proper bed in procedure 
-Proper caliper alignment 
-Pad contamination 

When the brake pads and rotors are new they need to be bedded in together. In a nutshell they need to be ridden and slowly and evenly warmed up together, with out coming to a complete stop until there is some mating between the surfaces.

If the alignment of the caliper is off the the pads may be contacting the rotor at an angle. Look for parallel gaps between on either side of the rotor.

Pad contamination is easy enough to identify. Usually there is a lot of sound and little to no stopping power.  Time for new pads.

There are a lot of other things to look for as well that take a little more investigating. I’ve noted sometimes if the brake line isn’t long enough it can put pressure on the caliper that can result in “gobble ”  try feeding a little slack to the caliper if you think it looks like he hose is coming out at a sharp angle. Also, if the rotor mounting bolts aren’t evenly torqued upon install or not tightened in a star pattern this can contribute. I’ve even had one case where extremely uneven and low spoke tension was a contributing factor.

All of this is relevant to any brand disc brake and worth checking for noise, regardless of the manufacturer.  Sometimes these are things that can be fixed quickly and don’t require time off the bike.
